newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong salutes China's Deng on funeral day.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong salutes China's Deng on funeral day.

text.p: Ships blasted horns, buses trailed black ribbons, train stations broadcast dirges and flags flew at half mast as Hong Kong saluted China's dead patriarch Deng Xiaoping at the time of his Beijing funeral on Tuesday.
Hong Kong's subway train network, the Mass Transit Railway, played sombre music at 38 of its stations for 10 minutes at 10 a.m. (0200 GMT) as the Beijing ceremony began.
The famed 109-year-old funicular Peak Tram, which scales the tropical slopes of Hong Kong Island to Victoria Peak, halted its red carriages in their tracks for one minute.

The fleets of Hong Kong Ferry and Star Ferry, which shuttle to and fro across the world's busiest harbour between Hong Kong Island and the mainland Kowloon Peninsula, blew their horns for one minute when the clock struck ten.
At the Central Ferry Pier in the British colony's financial district, taxi drivers blasted their klaxons in unison.
The China Motor Bus Co's double-decker buses were draped with black ribbons and white flowers, a Chinese mourning symbol.

The Hong Kong Stock Exchange broke with routine by not raising its company flag for the day, while the British and Hong Kong flags on the building flew at half-mast to mark Deng's funeral, Stock Exchange spokesman Henry Law said.
Hong Kong, a British colony for 150 years, will return to Chinese rule as a highly autonomous region at midnight on June 30, under Deng's "one country two systems" policy.
Under the policy, Hong Kong, a territory of 6.4 million people on the south China coast, can keep its freewheeling capitalist system for a further half century.
Chinese-funded firms in Hong Kong also paid their respects to Deng by stopping work and watching the live broadcast of the funeral carried on all the territory's television stations.
Staff at the Bank of China headquarters in the colony said they stopped work and watched the funeral on television.

Schools in the territory held moments of silence. Pupils at the well-known left-wing Pui Kiu Middle School, in North Point, staged a five-minute silence in front of a picture of Deng and a black and white banner with the words "Profound condolences to Mr Deng Xiaoping".
Most people filing through the MTR subway stations ignored the funeral dirges, while visitors to Hong Kong looked puzzled by the sombre music wafting from the public address system.
Chat Hesterman, an American who has been in the territory for six months, said he had no idea why the mourning music was being played at the Central MTR station.
Motoaki Goto, a Japanese businessman who has lived in Hong Kong for 18 years, said at the Central MTR station it was good that the territory paid its respects to Deng.

"Hong Kong will eventually be part of China," Goto told Reuters. "If Hong Kong people do not follow China's mentality, Hong Kong will not be able to adopt to the mainland's way of life in the future."
